title: Questions we can test: guess first, then try it

summary.text: Can a pencil lift a whole bottle of rice? You cannot know by thinking about it. You have to try it and watch. A question like this is a testable question: doing something shows the answer to anyone who looks. Other questions, like 'Which colour is the best?', have no test, because each person's answer is true for them. Your child sorts questions, makes predictions with reasons, tests them, and hears how two astronomers, Edmond Halley and Nicole-Reine Lepaute, predicted the return of a comet.
summary.art: A girl holding up a pencil with a plastic bottle full of rice hanging from it, her mouth open in surprise, while a woman beside her claps.

intro.hook: Here is a bottle full of rice and one pencil. Push the pencil into the rice. Can you lift the whole bottle by the pencil? What do you think, and why?
intro.text: You just made a prediction. A prediction is what you think will happen, and why, said before you try. Some questions can be answered by trying, like this one. Others cannot, like 'Is rice nicer than roti?' In this unit you learn to tell the two kinds apart. You make predictions, test them, and count what happens. A wrong prediction is useful too: it shows you which idea to change.
intro.art: A plastic bottle filled to the top with rice on a steel tray, a pencil lying beside it, and a child's hand hovering over it with a question mark above.

outcomes: By the end I can tell which questions we can test by trying and which we cannot, and say why.
By the end I can make a prediction and give a reason for it, before a test.
By the end I can do a test, count what happens, and say if my prediction was right.
By the end I can say what I learned when my prediction was wrong.
By the end I can say that some things, like a dropped spoon falling, can be predicted every time, and others, like one coin toss, cannot.
By the end I can tell how Halley and Lepaute predicted the return of a comet, and what it showed.

terms.meaning: A testable question is one you can answer by doing something and watching what happens. Anyone who does the same thing sees the same answer.
terms.example: 'Does a steel spoon sink in water?' is testable. Drop one in a tumbler of water and watch.
terms.art: A child dropping a steel spoon into a glass tumbler of water, with a tick mark beside it.

terms.meaning: A prediction is what you think will happen, and why, said before you try. It is a guess with a reason.
terms.example: 'The crumpled paper will land first, because it is a small ball and the air slows it less.'
terms.art: A girl holding a flat sheet of paper in one hand and a crumpled paper ball in the other, with a speech bubble showing a ball landing first.

terms.meaning: A test is something you do to find out if your prediction is right. You do it, watch carefully and write down what happened.
terms.example: Pushing a pencil into rice and lifting it is a test of the question 'Can a pencil lift a bottle of rice?'
terms.art: A hand lifting a pencil out of a rice bottle a little way above a steel tray.

terms.meaning: The result is what really happened in your test. You write it down, even when it is not what you predicted.
terms.example: 'The bottle lifted after 30 pokes' is a result.
terms.art: A child's notebook page with a drawing of a rice bottle hanging from a pencil, and the number 30 written beside it.

terms.meaning: An opinion is what one person likes, wants or feels is best. Two people can have different opinions, and both can be true for them.
terms.example: 'Idli is tastier than dosa' is an opinion. Your friend may think dosa is tastier.
terms.art: Two children at a table, one pointing at a plate of idli and one at a dosa, both smiling.

terms.meaning: Friction is the grip between two things that touch. The harder they press together, the stronger the grip.
terms.example: Your chappal does not slip on the road because of friction.
terms.art: A close-up of a rubber chappal sole on a rough road, with small arrows showing the grip.

explanations.concept: Questions we can test, and questions we can't
explanations.context: This card is about two kinds of questions: ones a test can answer, and ones it can't.
explanations.definition: A question is testable when you can do something, watch what happens, and get an answer that anyone else would also see.
explanations.description: 'Can a pencil lift a bottle of rice?' is testable. You try it, and everyone watching sees the same thing. 'Which colour is the best?' is an opinion, so no test can answer it. Some questions are not testable yet, like 'Is there life on a planet near another star?' Nobody can travel there today. Some questions are answered by asking, like 'When was Amma born?'
examples: Testable: 'Does a steel spoon sink in water?' Drop one in and see.
An opinion: 'Is a mango nicer than a banana?' Each person's answer is true for them.
Not testable yet: 'What is at the very edge of space?' Nobody can go there to look.
Answered by asking: 'What did Ammamma eat when she was small?' Ask her.
explanations.art: Four boxes on a page: a spoon sinking in water with a tick, a mango and a banana with two smiling faces, a dark starry sky with a question mark, and a grandmother talking to a child.

explanations.concept: A prediction is a guess with a reason
explanations.context: This card is about what a prediction is, and why we say the reason too.
explanations.definition: A prediction says what you think will happen in a test, and why you think so, before the test starts.
explanations.description: 'I think the bottle will fall' is a guess. 'I think the bottle will fall, because rice is loose and slippery' is a prediction, because it has a reason. If the bottle lifts, the reason shows which idea to change. Say your prediction before the test. After the test, anyone can say 'I knew it!'
examples: 'The ice will float, because I have seen ice floating in a glass of water.'
'The crumpled paper will land first, because it is smaller, so the air pushes it less.'
'It will rain today, because the sky is dark grey and the wind is cool.'
explanations.art: A girl writing on a slip of paper, 'I think it will fall because...', next to an untouched rice bottle.

explanations.concept: A wrong prediction still teaches you something
explanations.context: This card is about what to do when your prediction turns out wrong.
explanations.definition: When a result does not match a prediction, the idea behind the prediction needs to change.
explanations.description: Many people predict that a pencil cannot lift a bottle of rice. Then they see it lift. Their idea, 'rice is too loose to grip', was wrong for packed rice. Scientists are wrong often too. They write down what happened, change their idea, and test again.
examples: In 1835, a French thinker, Auguste Comte, wrote that people would never find out what stars are made of. Within about 30 years, scientists began to find out from starlight.
In the Rice Bottle Lift, loose rice lets the pencil slide out. That result tells you to try packing the rice.
explanations.art: A boy scratching his head as a rice bottle hangs from a pencil, with a crossed-out guess and a new guess written on a slip beside him.

explanations.concept: Why the rice held the pencil
explanations.context: This card explains the Rice Bottle Lift, after you have tried it.
explanations.definition: Rice grains pressed tightly together push hard on each other and on the pencil, and friction between them holds the pencil.
explanations.description: Loose rice has air gaps between the grains. The grains can slide past each other, so the pencil slides out. Each poke and tap pushes the grains closer and fills the gaps. Then they press hard on the pencil from every side. Friction is the grip between two things that touch, and it gets stronger when they press harder. Hundreds of grains each grip the pencil a little. Together they hold up the whole bottle.
examples: A tightly packed dabba of dal is hard to push a spoon into.
A gunny sack of rice stands up by itself when it is full and tight.
explanations.art: A cut-away drawing of a bottle with rice grains packed tightly around a pencil, with small arrows from the grains pressing on the pencil.

explanations.concept: Some things can be predicted every time, and some can't
explanations.context: This card is about the Sure or Not Sure tally, where you dropped a spoon and shook a coin.
explanations.definition: Some events happen the same way every time, so we can predict each one. Others change by chance, so we can only predict what happens over many tries.
explanations.description: A spoon you let go of falls down every single time, because the Earth pulls it. You can predict every drop. A coin shaken in your hands lands heads or tails by chance. Nobody can predict one shake, but over many shakes about half land heads. Weather is in between. Forecasters at the India Meteorological Department use measurements to predict rain. They are right often, but not always.
examples: Sure every time: a dropped spoon falls, and the Sun rises in the east.
Chance: one coin toss, one roll of a Ludo die.

Often right: the weather forecast for tomorrow. Anna Mani, a scientist from Kerala, made and improved weather instruments for the India Meteorological Department, so forecasters had better measurements.
Eclipses can be predicted years ahead. In 499 CE, Aryabhata wrote that a solar eclipse happens when the Moon covers the Sun, and a lunar eclipse when the Moon moves into the Earth's shadow.
explanations.art: A spoon falling with ten ticks beside it, and a coin in the air with a mix of ticks and crosses beside it.

explanations.concept: Can we test what it is like to be someone else?
explanations.context: This card is about a hard question: can a test show what another being feels?
explanations.description: Ants sense, remember and choose. You can test what an ant does: put sugar out and watch which way she goes. It is much harder to test what it is like, from the inside, to be that ant. Scientists argue about whether a test can ever show this.
examples: A test can show that a crow chooses the bigger piece of roti.
A test can show that a bean plant turns their leaves towards the window.

perspectives.who: Many scientists who study other animals
perspectives.explanation: What a being does tells us a lot about what they feel and think, just as we know a friend's feelings by what they do and say.
We can test what others do, but what it feels like inside them can never be checked from outside, not even for another person.

explanations.art: A girl lying on the floor looking closely at an ant carrying a sugar grain, with a thought bubble over the ant left blank.

agreed.text: A testable question is answered by doing something and watching what happens.
agreed.evidence: When anyone does the Rice Bottle Lift in the same way, with the rice packed tight, the bottle lifts. The result does not depend on who is watching.

agreed.text: A prediction must be said before the test.
agreed.evidence: After a result, it is easy to think 'I knew it'. Scientists write predictions down first, so that the test can really show if they were wrong.

agreed.text: One test can be a fluke, so we test again.
agreed.evidence: In the Lucky Blow test, you count the sixes with a blow and the sixes without. The two counts are often different just by chance. When you do the test again, the bigger count is often on the other side.

challenging.claim: Blowing on a die before you roll it brings more sixes.
challenging.who: A common belief in many games, in India and elsewhere
challenging.for: Sometimes a six comes right after a blow, and we remember those times.
challenging.against: Count the sixes in many rolls with a blow and many without. The counts come out about the same. We tend to remember the lucky times and forget the others.
challenging.context: This card is about a belief you can test with a Ludo die.

challenging.claim: Some questions can never be tested, like what the stars are made of.
challenging.who: Auguste Comte, a French thinker, in 1835
challenging.for: In 1835 nobody could travel to a star or bring back a piece of one.
challenging.against: In 1859 and 1860, Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen in Germany found that each kind of material gives out its own colours of light. Starlight carries those colours. In 1925, Cecilia Payne showed from starlight that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
challenging.context: This card is about a question that looked untestable and later became testable.

challenging.claim: A real scientific idea must be one that a test could prove wrong.
challenging.who: Karl Popper, a philosopher born in Austria, in the 1930s
challenging.for: If no test could ever show that an idea is wrong, the idea fits whatever happens. So it tells us nothing about what will happen.
challenging.against: Some scientists say ideas about the very start of the universe are still science, though nobody can test them yet. They hope tests will come later, as they did for the stars.
challenging.context: This card is about a big argument: does science need ideas that can be tested?

big_questions.q: If nobody can test which colour is the best, does that make the question silly?
big_questions.hint: Think about why people still ask it. What does your answer tell someone about you?

big_questions.q: Your prediction was wrong, but you learned something. Was it a good prediction or a bad one?
big_questions.hint: Think about the reason you gave. Did the wrong result show you which idea to change?

big_questions.q: A question nobody could test in 1835 was tested later. Which questions that we can't test today might be tested one day?
big_questions.hint: Think about the stars, the middle of the Earth, what it feels like to be an ant, or the start of everything.

big_questions.q: Why do you think people like to predict things, like rain, a cricket score or the end of a story?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you do when you know what is coming, and how a surprise feels.

story.title: Two Tumblers of Batter
story.note: Visakhapatnam is a city by the sea in Andhra Pradesh. Ammamma means mother's mother in Telugu, and mama means mother's brother. Ila, Kiran mama, Amma and Ammamma are made up. It is true that dosa batter rises much less in a fridge: the microbes that make it rise, bacteria and yeasts, work slowly in the cold.
text: Ila was seven. She lived on the fourth floor of a block of flats in Visakhapatnam, close enough to the sea to smell it when the wind blew. She lived with Amma and Ammamma, her grandmother.
That week, Kiran mama had come from Pune. He was Amma's younger brother. He was tall, he laughed loudly, and he was always sure he was right.

On Saturday evening, Ammamma ground rice and urad dal into a thick, white batter for the next morning's dosas. She poured it into a big steel vessel and set it on the shelf beside the stove, where the kitchen was warmest.
Kiran mama looked at it. 'Why leave it out?' he said. 'Put it in the fridge. The fridge keeps things fresh. It will rise just the same.'
Ammamma said nothing. She only smiled and looked at Ila.
Ila looked at the batter. In the morning it was always higher in the vessel, puffy, with tiny holes on top. She had never wondered why. Now she did.
'Does it rise the same in the fridge?' she said slowly. 'We could find out.'
'Find out how?' said Kiran mama.
'We test it,' said Ila. 'Ammamma, can I have two tumblers?'

Ammamma gave her two steel tumblers that were exactly the same. Ila poured batter into each one, up to the same height. Ammamma helped her slip a rubber band round each tumbler, right at the top of the batter.
'Before we test,' said Ammamma, 'each of you must make a prediction. What will happen, and why?'
Kiran mama folded his arms. 'Both will rise the same. Batter rises by itself. Cold or warm makes no difference.'
Ila thought hard. 'I think the shelf one will rise more,' she said. 'Because Ammamma always keeps it near the stove. She must have a reason.'
Ammamma wrote both predictions on the back of an old calendar page. Then one tumbler went into the fridge and one went on the warm shelf.
At dinner, Kiran mama ate three chapatis and said, 'Now here is a real question for you, Ila. Which is better, idli or dosa?'
'Dosa,' said Amma at once.
'Idli,' said Ammamma.
Ila laughed. 'We can't test that one,' she said. 'Amma likes dosa and Ammamma likes idli. They are both right, for themselves.'
Kiran mama raised his eyebrows. 'So the batter question is a different kind of question?'
'Yes,' said Ila. 'For the batter, we just look in the morning. Everyone will see the same thing.'

In the morning Ila ran to the kitchen before she even brushed her teeth. The tumbler on the shelf was full. The batter had risen far above the rubber band. It was puffed up and bubbly, and it smelled a little sour.
Then she opened the fridge. The batter in that tumbler sat almost exactly at its rubber band. It was smooth and flat, with hardly a bubble.
'Mama! Come and see!'
Kiran mama came in, yawning. He looked at the two tumblers for a long time. 'Well,' he said. 'I was wrong.'
'Your prediction helped, though,' said Ila. 'If you hadn't said it, we would never have tested it.'
Ammamma poured a ladle of the risen batter onto the hot tava. It spread into a thin circle and sizzled. 'Do you know why it rises?' she asked them both.

Neither of them did. So Ammamma explained. Batter is full of tiny living beings, too small to see, called microbes. All night they feed on the rice and dal, and they make gas. The gas makes the bubbles, and the bubbles push the batter up. In the warm kitchen they work fast. In the cold fridge they work very slowly.
'So the fridge does keep it fresh,' said Kiran mama. 'It keeps the microbes slow.'
'Yes,' said Ammamma. 'That is why we put the batter in the fridge after it has risen, not before.'
Ila ate her dosa. It was crisp at the edges and soft in the middle. She looked at the calendar page with the two predictions on it.
'Mama,' she said, 'let's test something else today.'
Kiran mama groaned, but he was smiling. 'Only if I get to predict first.'
story.epiphany: Ila found that some questions, like 'Does batter rise in the fridge?', can be answered by a test that everyone can see. Others, like 'Which is better, idli or dosa?', are opinions, and each person's answer is true for them.
ask: What were the two predictions, and what reason did each person give?
Why did Ila use two tumblers that were exactly the same, with rubber bands at the same height?
Why couldn't anyone test 'Which is better, idli or dosa?'
Kiran mama was wrong. How did his prediction still help?

games.title: Test It or Not? the question card game
games.players: 2 or more players, or with a parent. A grown-up reads the cards for a child who is still learning to read.
games.context: This is a card game about questions. You sort question cards into two piles: questions we can test by trying, and questions we can't. Then you check the back of the card.

printables.title: 2 pile cards
items: WE CAN TEST IT BY TRYING
WE CAN'T TEST IT BY TRYING

items.f: Does a steel spoon sink in water?
items.b: We can test it. Drop a spoon in a tumbler of water and watch.

items.f: Which colour is the most beautiful?
items.b: We can't test it. It is an opinion. Each person's answer is true for them.

items.f: Does ice float in water?
items.b: We can test it. Put an ice cube in a glass of water.

items.f: Is a mango nicer than a banana?
items.b: We can't test it. It is an opinion.

items.f: Does salt disappear when you stir it into water?
items.b: We can test it. Stir a pinch of salt into a tumbler of water and look.

items.f: Is there life on a planet near another star?
items.b: We can't test it yet. Nobody can go there today. One day we might.

items.f: Does a crumpled paper ball fall faster than a flat sheet?
items.b: We can test it. Drop both together from the same height.

items.f: Which song is the best song?
items.b: We can't test it. It is an opinion.

items.f: Do ants come to a drop of sugar water?
items.b: We can test it. Put a drop near where you see ants, and watch.

items.f: What is at the very edge of space?
items.b: We can't test it yet. Nobody can travel that far.

items.f: Can you hear a tap through a table better than through the air?
items.b: We can test it. Put your ear on the table while someone taps the far end, then listen with your head up.

items.f: Is Diwali more fun than Onam?
items.b: We can't test it. It is an opinion. Different families love different festivals.

items.f: Does a wet hanky dry faster under the fan?
items.b: We can test it. Wet two hankies, put one under the fan and one away from it, and feel them after an hour.

items.f: Is it better to be a cat or a dog?
items.b: We can't test it. It is an opinion, and nobody can be both to compare.

items.f: Do bean seeds sprout faster when they are soaked first?
items.b: We can test it. Soak some seeds and not others, plant them all, and watch for a week.

items.f: What will I dream about tonight?
items.b: We can't test it before it happens. Nobody can know a dream before it comes.

rules: Put the two pile cards face up on the floor, side by side.
Shuffle the question cards and put them in a pile, face down.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out.
Put it under the pile card you choose, and say why.
If it is a test question, also say how you would test it.
Turn the card over and read the back. If you were right, keep the card.
If you were wrong, put the card at the bottom of the pile.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most cards wins.

Put it in a tumbler and watch.

flow.do: Take turns until the pile is finished. Ask for a reason with every card.
flow.say: Your turn. Read it, choose a pile, and tell me why.
flow.kid: Take a card. Choose a pile. Say why.
flow.parent: If your child puts an opinion card under 'test it', ask: 'What would you do to test it? Would everyone get the same answer?'

games.title: Guess First: the quick test card game
games.players: 2 or more players, or with a parent. Works alone too: keep your own score.
games.context: This is a prediction game. Each card is a quick test you can do at home. Before you do it, every player predicts what will happen and says why. Then you do the test and see who was right.

items.f: Drop a steel spoon into a tumbler of water. Will it sink or float?
items.b: It sinks.

items.f: Put an ice cube into a tumbler of water. Will it sink or float?
items.b: It floats, with most of it under the water.

items.f: Hold a flat sheet of paper and a crumpled ball of paper at the same height. Let go together. Which lands first?
items.b: The crumpled ball lands first. The air slows the flat sheet more.

items.f: Hold a strip of paper just under your bottom lip, so it hangs down. Blow hard straight ahead. Will the strip go down, stay still or lift up?
items.b: It lifts up into the moving air. Scientists explain this in more than one way.

items.f: Put one drop of water on newspaper and one on a steel plate. Which one stays on top as a drop?
items.b: The drop on the steel plate stays on top. The newspaper soaks the water up.

items.f: Half fill a tumbler with water. Tilt it a little. Will the top of the water tilt with the tumbler, or stay flat?
items.b: The top of the water stays flat, even when the tumbler tilts.

items.f: Stir a pinch of salt into a tumbler of water. Will you still see the salt after one minute?
items.b: No. The salt dissolves: it breaks into pieces too small to see, but it is still there. Taste a drop to check.

items.f: Stuff a dry tissue into the bottom of an empty glass. Push the glass straight down, upside down, into a bowl of water. Will the tissue get wet?
items.b: No. Air is trapped inside the glass, and it keeps the water out.

items.f: Look at your face in the back of a shiny steel spoon. Will you be the right way up or upside down?
items.b: The right way up. Now try the front of the spoon, held at arm's length: you are upside down.

items.f: Put a lemon in a bowl of water. Will it sink or float?
items.b: Most lemons float. The peel is full of tiny air pockets.

printables.title: Prediction score sheet
items: Points: 1 for a right prediction, 1 for a good reason

rules: Put the cards in a pile, face down. Put the things the cards need nearby: a tumbler of water, a steel spoon, paper, a steel plate, salt, a glass, a bowl of water, an ice cube and a lemon.
Take the top card and read the front aloud. Do not look at the back.
Every player says a prediction and a reason. Write them on the score sheet.
Do the test together and watch closely.
Read the back of the card to check.
Each player gets 1 point for a right prediction and 1 point for giving a reason.
A wrong prediction with a reason still gets 1 point.
After all 10 cards, the player with the most points wins.

check.q: You predicted the lemon would sink, but it floated. What gets you a point?

check.why: In this game a reason always earns a point, even when the prediction is wrong. A reason shows which idea to change. Pretending is never allowed, because then the test can't teach you anything.

experiments.title: The Rice Bottle Lift: can a pencil lift a bottle of rice?
experiments.context: In this experiment you fill a plastic bottle with rice and push a pencil into it. You predict whether the pencil can lift the bottle, and how many pokes it will take. Then you test it.
experiments.question: Can a pencil pushed into rice lift the whole bottle? Does it work better when the rice is loose, or packed tight?
experiments.predict: Look at the bottle of rice and the pencil. Will the pencil lift the bottle, or slide out? Why do you think so? If we poke and press the rice many times, how many pokes will it take before it lifts?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same bottle, the same rice and the same pencil every time. Only one thing changes: how tightly the rice is packed. Lift slowly and the same way each time.

materials.item: 1 small plastic bottle with a narrow neck, about 200 to 500 ml, like a water or juice bottle, with the cap off
uncooked rice, enough to fill the bottle to the very top (about 2 cups for a 500 ml bottle)
1 pencil, or a wooden chopstick or ice-cream stick if the neck is wide
a paper cone made from a sheet of newspaper, or a funnel
a steel tray or a big plate to catch spilled rice
paper and a pencil for the results

experiments.safety: Use a plastic bottle, never glass. Lift it only a hand's width above the tray, so it falls softly if it slips.

schedule.what: Fill a bottle with rice, predict, and test whether a pencil can lift it, with loose rice and with packed rice.

experiments.record: Draw the bottle hanging from the pencil, or falling off it. Write your prediction, the number of pokes and what happened for each try.

setup.art: A hand pushing a pencil down into the rice in the bottle, with grains spilling onto the tray.
setup.caption: 2. Push the pencil in and try to lift.

setup.art: A child tapping the bottom of the rice bottle on the tray, with small lines showing the tapping.
setup.caption: 3. Poke, tap and top up the rice to pack it tight.

setup.art: A plastic bottle of rice hanging from a pencil held by a child's hand, just above a steel tray.
setup.caption: 4. Lift slowly. Does the bottle come up?

flow.do: 1. Put the bottle on the tray. 2. Your child pours rice in through the paper cone, up to the very top. 3. Do not tap or press it yet.
flow.say: Let's fill this bottle right to the top with rice. Pour gently. Don't press it down yet.
flow.kid: Fill the bottle to the top with rice. Pour gently.

flow.do: Ask for a prediction and a reason. Make your own prediction too. Write both down.
flow.say: If you push the pencil in and pull it up, will the bottle come up too? Why do you think so? I'll say my prediction too.
flow.kid: Will the pencil lift the bottle? Why do you think so?

good: No, because rice is loose and slippery.
No, the bottle is too heavy for a pencil.
Yes, because the rice will squeeze the pencil.

flow.parent: Any prediction is fine, as long as it has a reason. Do not hint at the answer.

flow.do: 1. Your child pushes the pencil straight down, deep into the rice. 2. They hold the bottle's neck with one hand and the pencil with the other. 3. They let go of the bottle and lift the pencil slowly.
flow.say: Push the pencil in, deep. Now let go of the bottle and lift the pencil slowly. What happens?
flow.kid: Push the pencil in deep. Let go of the bottle. Lift slowly.
flow.parent: With loose rice the pencil nearly always slides out. That is a real result. Write it down.

flow.do: Ask for a new prediction: how many pokes until it lifts? Write the number.
flow.say: Now we'll poke the pencil in and out, and tap the bottle, to press the rice tight. How many pokes do you think it will take before it lifts? Why?
flow.kid: We will poke and tap. How many pokes until it lifts? Guess a number.

good: Ten, because the rice needs to get tight.
A hundred, because it was very loose.

flow.do: 1. Your child pokes the pencil in and out, counting aloud. 2. Every 10 pokes, tap the bottle on the tray 5 times. 3. Top up the rice to the very top. 4. After every 10 pokes, leave the pencil in and try a slow lift.
flow.say: Poke in and out, and count. After every ten pokes, tap the bottle and fill it up again. Then push the pencil in and try lifting.
flow.kid: Poke and count. After every ten pokes, tap the bottle and add rice. Then try to lift.
flow.parent: The rice gets lower as it packs, so keep adding rice to the very top. Many bottles lift after 20 to 50 pokes, but it varies. A rough wooden chopstick or ice-cream stick grips better than a shiny painted pencil. If yours has not lifted after 60 pokes, use a narrower bottle or fill it fuller.

flow.do: 1. When the bottle lifts, write the number of pokes. 2. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: It lifted! How many pokes did it take? Was your prediction right? What do you think made the difference?
flow.kid: How many pokes did it take? Was your guess right? What made the bottle lift?

ask.q: What made it work the second time?
good: The rice was squashed tight round the pencil.
There were no gaps, so the rice held on.
Tapping pushed the rice together.

flow.parent: Listen to your child's reason before you explain anything.

flow.do: Pull the pencil out. Ask for one more prediction. Then push it back in and lift.
flow.say: Now I'll pull the pencil out. If I push it back in, will it lift straight away, or need many pokes again? Why?
flow.kid: Pull the pencil out, then push it back in. Will it lift at once? Why?
flow.parent: It usually lifts at once, because the rice is still packed tight. If not, it needs only a few pokes.

check.q: The rice was loose and the pencil slid out. Then you packed it tight and it lifted. What changed?
options: How tightly the rice was packed
check.why: Only the packing changed. The same pencil and bottle were used every time, so the packing must be what made the difference. If you chose the pencil or the bottle, look again: they stayed the same.

flow.do: Now explain, using your child's own words first.
flow.say: Loose rice has air gaps, so the grains slide. Poking and tapping squeezed them together. Then they pressed hard on the pencil. That grip is called friction. Many grains each gripped a little, and together they held the bottle.
flow.kid: Squashed rice presses on the pencil. That grip is called friction. Many grains together held the bottle.
flow.parent: Pour the rice back into the tin afterwards. It is clean and can still be cooked.

experiments.title: The Lucky Blow: does blowing on a die bring more sixes?
experiments.context: In this experiment you test a belief many people have: that blowing on a die before you roll it brings a six. You roll 30 times with a blow and 30 times without, and count the sixes.
experiments.question: Does blowing on a die before rolling it give more sixes than not blowing?
experiments.predict: Will you get more sixes when you blow on the die, fewer, or about the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same die, the same hand and the same tray every time. Shake the die in your closed hand the same way and roll it onto the tray. Only one thing changes: blowing on it or not.

materials.item: 1 die from a Ludo or snakes-and-ladders game
a steel tray or plate with a rim, to roll onto
paper and a pencil for tally marks

setup.art: A child blowing into a closed fist holding a Ludo die, above a steel tray.
setup.caption: 1. Blow on the die, then roll it onto the tray.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with two columns, 'Blow' and 'No blow', and tally marks in groups of five.
setup.caption: 2. Make a tally mark for each six.

flow.do: 1. Draw two columns on paper: 'Blow' and 'No blow'. 2. Ask for a prediction and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: Some people blow on a die to get a six. Does it work? What do you predict, and why?
flow.kid: Does blowing on the die bring a six? Guess, and say why.

good: Yes, because people do it in games.
No, because blowing does not change how the die falls.
Maybe, I am not sure.

flow.do: 1. Your child blows on the die in their closed hand, shakes it and rolls it onto the tray. 2. Count 30 rolls. 3. Make a tally mark in 'Blow' for each six.
flow.say: Blow on the die, shake it and roll it. Do this thirty times. Each time it shows six, make a mark in the Blow column.
flow.kid: Blow on the die, shake it and roll it. Do this thirty times. Mark each six.
flow.parent: Count the rolls on your fingers or with pebbles, so you stop at exactly 30.

flow.do: Do 30 more rolls the same way, without blowing. Mark each six in 'No blow'.
flow.say: Now roll 30 more times, exactly the same way, but without blowing. Mark each six.
flow.kid: Roll thirty more times with the same shake, but no blowing. Mark each six.

flow.do: Count both columns. Ask what the counts show.
flow.say: How many sixes with a blow? How many without? Is the difference big or small? Do you think it would be the same if we did it again?
flow.kid: Count the sixes in each column. Which has more? Is it a big difference?
flow.parent: Each count is usually somewhere between 2 and 9, and the two counts are rarely exactly the same. A small difference is just chance. If you have time, do both again: the bigger count often swaps sides.

check.q: Blowing gave 6 sixes and not blowing gave 4. What does that show?
options: The difference is small, so it may be chance. We need to test again
check.why: With a die, the number of sixes changes by chance each time. A difference of 2 in 30 rolls is small. Testing again shows whether it was a fluke. If you chose 'Blowing works', try another 30 rolls of each and see.

flow.do: Ask your child: does blowing help, what do the marks show, and why?
flow.say: So, does blowing help? What is your evidence? Why do you think the die did that?
flow.kid: Does blowing help? What did your marks show?

activities.title: Sure or Not Sure? Ten drops and ten coin shakes
activities.context: In this activity you predict two things ten times each: will a dropped spoon fall, and will a shaken coin land heads? You count how many predictions were right.

materials.item: a steel spoon
a coin
a cushion or a bed to drop things onto
paper and a pencil for ticks and crosses

setup.art: A child holding a steel spoon above a cushion, with a row of ten ticks drawn on paper beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Predict, then drop the spoon. Ten times.

setup.art: A child shaking a coin in cupped hands above a bed, with a row of ticks and crosses drawn on paper.
setup.caption: 2. Predict heads or tails, then shake and drop the coin. Ten times.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the spoon above the cushion. 2. Before each drop, they say what will happen. 3. They let go. 4. Tick if the prediction was right. 5. Do it 10 times.
flow.say: Before you let go, tell me: what will the spoon do? Now let go. Do it ten times.
flow.kid: Say what the spoon will do. Let go. Do it ten times.

flow.do: 1. Your child shakes the coin in cupped hands. 2. Before each drop, they say 'heads' or 'tails'. 3. They drop it on the bed. 4. Tick if right, cross if wrong. 5. Do it 10 times.
flow.say: Say heads or tails first. Now shake the coin and drop it. Were you right? Do it ten times.
flow.kid: Say heads or tails. Shake the coin and drop it. Tick if you were right, cross if you were wrong.

flow.do: Count the ticks in each row. Ask which one your child could predict.
flow.say: How many spoon predictions were right? How many coin ones? Which could you predict every time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count your ticks. Which could you predict every time? Why?
flow.parent: Nearly every child gets all 10 spoon drops right. Coin guesses are usually somewhere between 3 and 7 right. The Earth pulls the spoon down every time. A coin lands by chance.

check.q: Can anyone predict every coin shake right?
options: No, each shake lands by chance
check.why: A coin lands heads or tails by chance, so nobody can predict one shake for sure. Over many shakes, about half come out heads. If you chose 'yes', look at your crosses: you tried hard and still got some wrong.

activities.title: Turn It Into a Test
activities.context: In this activity you take a question that can't be tested, and change it into one that can. Then you do one of the tests.

materials.item: 3 sheets of newspaper or used paper for paper planes
paper and a pencil

setup.art: Two folded paper planes on a floor, one with a pointed nose and one with a wide nose, and a strip of tape on the floor as a start line.
setup.caption: 1. Make two different paper planes.

setup.art: A girl throwing a paper plane from a tape line on the floor, with a slipper marking where the other plane landed.
setup.caption: 2. Throw each one from the same line. Which goes further?

flow.do: Read out this question: 'Which paper plane is the best?' Ask if it can be tested.
flow.say: Here is a question: which paper plane is the best? Can we test that? What does 'best' mean?
flow.kid: Which paper plane is best? Can you test that? What does best mean?

good: The one that flies furthest.
The one that stays up longest.
The prettiest one.

flow.parent: The prettiest is an opinion. The furthest or the longest in the air can be tested.

flow.do: Help your child change 'Which paper plane is the best?' into a test question. Write it down.
flow.say: Let's make 'Which paper plane is the best?' into a test question. Which plane flies further when we throw from the same line?
flow.kid: Turn 'Which paper plane is best?' into a test question: which plane flies further from the same line?

flow.do: 1. Fold two different planes. 2. Ask for a prediction and a reason. 3. Throw each one 3 times from the same line. 4. Mark where each lands with a slipper.
flow.say: Which plane will go further? Why? Now throw each one three times from the line. Throw the same way each time.
flow.kid: Which plane will go further? Why? Throw each three times.
flow.parent: Throw each plane three times, because one throw can be a fluke.

flow.do: Ask your child to change one more question into a test.
flow.say: Now you try. 'Is my ball the best ball?' How could we turn that into a test?
flow.kid: Is my ball the best ball? Turn it into a test question.

ask.q: What test question could we ask?
good: Which ball bounces highest?
Which ball rolls furthest down the corridor?

activities.title: Guess the Grains: predict, count, predict again
activities.context: In this activity you predict how many chana are in one spoonful, then count them. Then you use what you found to predict how many are in two spoonfuls.

materials.item: about 1 cup of dry kabuli chana, rajma or any big dry beans
a big spoon
a steel plate
paper and a pencil

setup.art: A big spoon full of dry chana held over a steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. Predict how many chana are in one spoonful.

setup.art: Chana arranged in small groups of ten on a steel plate, with a child counting the groups.
setup.caption: 2. Count them in groups of ten.

flow.do: Your child scoops one level spoonful of chana. Ask for a prediction and a reason.
flow.say: How many chana are in this spoon? Make a prediction. Why that number?
flow.kid: How many chana in the spoon? Guess. Why that number?

flow.do: Tip the spoon onto the plate. Your child counts the chana into groups of ten. Write the number.
flow.say: Let's count them in groups of ten. How many groups? How many left over?
flow.kid: Count them in tens. How many?

flow.do: Ask for a new prediction: how many in two level spoonfuls? Ask for the reason.
flow.say: Now you know how many are in one spoon. How many will be in two spoons? Why?
flow.kid: How many in two spoons? Use what you counted.

good: One spoon had 25, so two spoons will have about 50.
Double, because it is two spoons.

flow.do: Scoop two level spoonfuls, count them, and compare both predictions with the counts.
flow.say: Count again. Which prediction was closer, your first one or your second one? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count again. Which guess was closer? Why?
flow.parent: The second prediction is usually much closer, because it was built on a count. Two spoons will not be exactly double, because each spoonful is a little different.

projects.title: My Prediction Diary: five days of guesses
projects.context: In this project you make one prediction every morning for five days, with a reason, and check it later the same day. At the end you see which kinds of things were easy or hard to predict.

materials.item: a small notebook or 5 sheets of paper
a pencil and crayons

schedule.what: Morning: predict what the sky will look like at lunchtime, and why. At lunch: look and tick or cross.
Morning: predict how many birds you will see from the window in two minutes after lunch. After lunch: count them.
Morning: predict what time the evening lights will need to be switched on. Evening: check the clock.
Morning: predict which of two wet hankies, one under the fan and one in a corner, will dry first. Check every hour.
Choose your own prediction. Then look back over the week: which predictions were right? Which were hardest?

projects.record: One page a day: my prediction, my reason, what happened, and a tick or a cross. On the last page, draw the prediction you were proudest of.

setup.art: A small notebook open on a table, with a page saying 'My prediction', 'My reason', 'What happened', and a crayon drawing of a cloudy sky.
setup.caption: 1. Each morning, write a prediction and a reason.

setup.art: A child at a window counting birds on a rooftop, holding a notebook with tally marks.
setup.caption: 2. Later the same day, check and tick or cross.

flow.do: Day 1 morning: your child predicts what the sky will look like at lunchtime and gives a reason. At lunch, check together.
flow.say: What will the sky look like at lunchtime? Sunny, cloudy or rainy? Why do you think so? We'll check at lunch.
flow.kid: What will the sky be like at lunch? Why? Check at lunch.

flow.do: Day 2, morning: your child predicts how many birds they will see from the window in two minutes after lunch. After lunch, count them.
flow.say: How many birds will you see from the window in two minutes after lunch? Why that number?
flow.kid: How many birds will you see in two minutes? Guess, then count.

flow.do: Day 3, morning: your child predicts what time the lights will need to be switched on in the evening. In the evening, check the clock.
flow.say: When will it get dark enough to switch on the lights? What time do you predict? Why?
flow.kid: What time will we need the lights? Guess. Check tonight.

flow.do: Day 4: wet two hankies the same amount. Hang one under the fan and one in a corner away from the fan. Your child predicts which will dry first, then feels them every hour.
flow.say: Which hanky will dry first? Why? Let's feel them every hour.
flow.kid: Which hanky will dry first? Why? Feel them every hour.

flow.do: Day 5: your child picks their own prediction. Then look back at all five pages together.
flow.say: Pick your own prediction today. Then let's look at the week. Which ones were right? Which were hardest to predict? Why?
flow.kid: Make your own prediction. Then look at your week. Which were hardest?

challenges.title: Fewest Pokes: make the rice grip faster
challenges.context: This is a challenge for after the Rice Bottle Lift. Can you make a pencil lift a bottle of rice with fewer pokes than it took then?
challenges.problem: In the Rice Bottle Lift, you counted how many pokes it took before the bottle lifted. Can you make it lift with fewer pokes?
constraints: Use rice and a pencil or stick.
Lift the bottle only a hand's width above a tray.
Predict your number of pokes before each try, and say why.
general: Fill the bottle right to the very top, so there is no space for the rice to move.
Tap the bottle on the tray many times before you start poking.
creative: Use a narrower bottle, so the rice is squeezed closer to the pencil.
Use a rougher stick, like a wooden chopstick, which has more grip than a smooth pencil.
Try dal or sabudana instead of rice, and predict first which will grip best.
challenges.your_turn: Choose one change. Predict how many pokes it will take, and why. Then test it and write the number.

setup.art: Two plastic bottles of rice, one wide and one narrow, side by side on a steel tray, with a pencil and a chopstick.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one change to try.

setup.art: A child writing a number on a slip of paper beside a rice bottle with a chopstick in it.
setup.caption: 2. Predict the pokes, then test.

flow.do: Read the problem to your child. Remind them of their poke count from the Rice Bottle Lift.
flow.say: In the Rice Bottle Lift it took this many pokes. Can you make the bottle lift with fewer? What could you change?
flow.kid: In the Rice Bottle Lift it took many pokes. Can you make the bottle lift with fewer?

flow.do: Your child chooses one change. They predict the number of pokes and give a reason.
flow.say: What will you change? How many pokes will it take now? Why?
flow.kid: Pick one change. Guess how many pokes it will take, and say why.

flow.do: Your child fills the bottle and tests the change, counting pokes. Write the number.
flow.say: Fill it, poke and count. Try a slow lift every ten pokes.
flow.kid: Fill the bottle. Poke and count. Try to lift after every ten pokes.

flow.do: Compare the new count with the count from the Rice Bottle Lift. Ask why it was different.
flow.say: Was it fewer pokes? Was your prediction close? Why do you think that change helped, or didn't?
flow.kid: Did it take fewer pokes? Was your guess close? Why?

quiz.p: Which question can you test by trying?
opts: Does a steel spoon sink in water?
Is Holi more fun than Pongal?
quiz.why: You can drop a spoon in water and everyone will see it sink. The other two are opinions: each person's answer is true for them.

quiz.p: 'Idli is tastier than dosa.' What kind of sentence is that?
quiz.why: It is what one person likes. Someone else may like dosa more, and they are right for themselves.

opts: I think the ice will float, because ice in my drink floats.
quiz.why: A prediction says what you think will happen, and why, before the test. 'The ice floated' is a result, after the test.

quiz.p: When should you say your prediction?
quiz.why: A prediction comes before the test, so the test can show if it was right. After a test, anyone can say 'I knew it.'

quiz.p: In the Rice Bottle Lift, the pencil slid out of loose rice. What made it lift later?
opts: Packing the rice tight by poking and tapping
quiz.why: Packed rice presses hard on the pencil, and friction holds it. Loose rice has gaps, so the grains slide.

quiz.p: You predicted the lemon would sink. It floated. What is the best thing to do?
opts: Write down that it floated, and think about why
Pretend you said it would float
quiz.why: A wrong prediction shows which idea to change. Now you can wonder what makes a lemon float.

quiz.p: Which can you predict right every single time?
opts: A spoon you let go of will fall
quiz.why: The Earth pulls a spoon down every time. A coin and a die land by chance.

quiz.p: If blowing on a die gave 6 sixes and not blowing gave 5, that proves blowing works.
quiz.why: False. Counts like these change by chance. A difference of 1 is tiny. You would need to test many more times to see if there is a real difference.

quiz.p: Comets were seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682. They all moved the same way across the sky, and came about 76 years apart. What is a good prediction?
opts: It is one comet coming back, so it will return about 76 years after 1682
quiz.why: The same path and the same gap of years suggest it is one comet that keeps coming back. A good prediction uses a pattern like this, and then a test can check it.

quiz.p: A comet comes back about every 76 years. On its trip it passes near big planets like Jupiter and Saturn. Why might it come back a little later than expected?
opts: The pull of the big planets can slow it down
quiz.why: Big planets pull on things that pass near them. Working out these pulls makes a prediction more exact.

items.p: Sort these questions into two groups. Circle the test questions in green and the opinion questions in blue.
cats: We can test it by trying
items: Does ice melt in the sun?
We can test it by trying
We can test it by trying
Does a ball roll faster down a steep slope?
We can test it by trying
items.why: A test question can be answered by doing something and watching. An opinion is what a person likes, so each person's answer is true for them.

items.p: Someone says, 'The crumpled paper will land first.' What should they add to make it a prediction?
opts: A reason: because it is a small ball
items.why: A prediction has a reason. The reason shows what the person thinks is going on, so the test can check it.

items.p: Draw the Rice Bottle Lift. Show the bottle, the rice and the pencil when the bottle lifted.
items.a: A drawing of a bottle full of rice hanging from a pencil held by a hand.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the rice right up to the top and the pencil deep inside it.
items.art: An empty box with a small tray drawn at the bottom.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it: before the Rice Bottle Lift, what did you predict? Was it right?
items.a: For example: I predicted the bottle would fall, because rice is loose. I was wrong when the rice was packed tight, because then the bottle lifted.
items.why: A strong answer gives the prediction, the reason, and what really happened.

items.p: Draw a line from each question to how you could find out.
pairs: Nobody can test it. It is an opinion
Is there life near another star?
items.why: Some questions need a test, some need asking, some are opinions, and some can't be tested yet.

items.p: A prediction that turns out wrong is wasted.
items.why: False. A wrong prediction shows which idea needs to change. Scientists learn a lot from wrong predictions.

items.p: In the Sure or Not Sure activity, you drop a spoon 10 times and predict right every time. You shake a coin 10 times and predict right 4 times. How many coin predictions were wrong?
items.why: 10 take away 4 is 6. Coin shakes land by chance, so many guesses are wrong.

items.p: Three of these are test questions. Which one is an opinion?
opts: Does a pebble sink in water?
Is a lemon prettier than a lime?
items.why: Whether a lemon is prettier is what one person feels. The other three can be tested with a bowl of water.

items.p: In the Lucky Blow test, why do we roll 30 times each, and not just once?
opts: One roll can be a fluke
items.why: A die lands by chance, so one roll tells us almost nothing. Many rolls show what usually happens.

items.p: Draw something you could test at home. Then say your test question, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: A drawing of something to test, with a question like 'Does a lemon float?'
items.why: A strong answer is a question that a test can answer, where everyone would see the same result.
items.art: A blank box with a small magnifying glass in one corner.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it: 'Which fruit is the best?' Why can't a test answer this?
items.a: For example: because everyone likes different fruits. My best fruit is mango, but my friend's is banana.
items.why: A strong answer says it is an opinion, and that different people's answers are all true for them.

items.p: Two girls in Kolkata, Mitali and Rumki, predict what happens when you push a pencil into a bottle of rice and lift it.

views.says: The bottle will come up, because the rice will hold the pencil.
The pencil will slide out, because the rice is loose and there are gaps.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you saw in the Rice Bottle Lift. Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer: Rumki is right for loose rice, because the grains slide. Mitali is right once the rice is packed tight, because then it grips the pencil. Both are right, in different cases.
items.why: Both girls have part of the answer. The test showed that it depends on how tightly the rice is packed.

items.p: Someone says, 'Batter rises the same in the fridge.' Say how you could test this, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: For example: put the same amount of batter in two tumblers, mark the top with a rubber band, put one in the fridge and one on a shelf, and look in the morning.
items.why: A strong answer uses two tumblers that are the same, changes only where they are kept, and says what to look at.

items.p: Put these steps of a test in order.
items: Make a prediction and give a reason
a: Make a prediction and give a reason
items.why: First you ask a question. Then you make a prediction with a reason, before testing. Then you do the test and write down the result.

items.p: We can never visit a star. But each material gives out its own colours of light. How could we still find out what stars are made of?
opts: By looking at the colours in starlight
We can never know anything about it
By bringing back a piece of a star
items.why: Each material gives out its own pattern of colours. Matching the colours in starlight to these patterns shows that stars are mostly hydrogen and helium.

items.p: Fill the gap: The grip between two things that touch is called ________.
items.why: Friction held the pencil in the packed rice. It gets stronger when things press harder together.

items.p: Draw the rice grains in loose rice and in packed rice, around a pencil. Show where the gaps are.
items.a: Loose rice drawn with spaces between grains. Packed rice drawn with grains touching each other and the pencil.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that packed grains touch the pencil all round, so they grip it.
items.art: Two empty circles side by side, each with a pencil drawn down the middle.

items.p: Some questions that could not be tested long ago can be tested today.
items.why: True. What the stars are made of could not be tested in 1835, but it was tested later using starlight.

items.p: In Guess the Grains, your second prediction was probably closer. Say why, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: For example: because I had counted one spoon first, so I knew about how many were in a spoon.
items.why: A strong answer says the second prediction used evidence from the first count.

items.p: Forecasters say it will probably rain tomorrow. It doesn't. What does that show?
opts: Weather can be predicted often, but not every time
items.why: Weather depends on many things that keep changing. Forecasters use measurements and are right often, but not always.

items.p: Sort these into 'Sure every time' and 'Chance each time'.
items: Ice melts in a hot room
One die roll shows a six
items.why: Things that always happen the same way can be predicted each time. Coins and dice land by chance.

items.p: Think of a question nobody can test today. Say why it can't be tested, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: For example: 'Is there life near another star?' We can't go there yet.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real reason: too far, too long ago, or too small to see with the tools we have.

applications: Weather forecasters at the India Meteorological Department predict rain and storms, so fishers know when the sea is unsafe.
Doctors predict when a baby will be born, from how big the baby is in a scan.
Astronomers predict eclipses years ahead, so people know when to look.
Engineers test a new bridge design with a small model before they build the real one.
Cooks predict how long rice will take, then check by pressing a grain.

open_questions.q: Will we ever be able to predict earthquakes?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can say which places are more likely to have earthquakes. Nobody can yet predict the day or hour of one.

open_questions.q: Is there life on planets around other stars?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found thousands of planets around other stars. They are looking for signs of life in the light from some of them, but nobody knows yet.

open_questions.q: Can a test ever show what it feels like to be an ant or a crow?
open_questions.why_open: We can test what ants and crows do, and that tells us they sense, remember and choose. Scientists and philosophers still argue about whether any test can show what their life feels like from the inside.

maths.problem: In the Lucky Blow test, you get 6 sixes with a blow and 4 sixes without, in 30 rolls each. How many more sixes did blowing give? Does that prove blowing works?
maths.answer: 2 more. No, that does not prove it.
maths.explain: 6 take away 4 is 2. But a die lands by chance, so counts of sixes change every time. A difference of 2 is small. You need to test again to see if it was a fluke.
maths.context: This is about the Lucky Blow test, where you rolled a die 30 times with a blow and 30 times without.
maths.why_maths: Counting tally marks lets us compare two results, and thinking about the size of the difference stops us being fooled by luck.

maths.problem: In the Sure or Not Sure activity, one child predicted 10 coin shakes and got 5 right. A second child got 7 right. Is the second child better at predicting coins?
maths.answer: No. Both got about half right, which is what chance gives.
maths.explain: A coin lands by chance, so over 10 shakes anyone gets about half right, sometimes a few more, sometimes a few fewer. 5 and 7 are both near half of 10. If the second child tries again, they may get 4.
maths.context: This is about the Sure or Not Sure activity, where you predicted heads or tails 10 times.
maths.why_maths: Knowing that half of 10 is 5 helps us see whether a result is just chance or something more.

maths.problem: In Guess the Grains, one spoonful had 23 chana. Predict how many are in two spoonfuls. The real count was 45. How close was the prediction?
maths.answer: Predict 46. It was 1 more than the real count.
maths.explain: 23 and 23 make 46. The real count was 45, and 46 take away 45 is 1. So the prediction was only 1 away, because it used the first count.
maths.context: This is about Guess the Grains, where you counted chana in one spoon, then predicted two spoons.
maths.why_maths: Adding the first count to itself turns a wild guess into a prediction built on evidence.

maths.problem: In the Rice Bottle Lift, your first prediction was that the bottle would lift after 5 pokes. It took 30. The next time you predicted 25, and it took 20. Which prediction was closer?
maths.explain: From 5 to 30 is 25 pokes away. From 20 to 25 is only 5 pokes away. 5 is less than 25, so the second prediction was much closer. It was closer because it used the first result.
maths.context: This is about the Rice Bottle Lift, where you counted pokes until a pencil could lift a bottle of rice.
maths.why_maths: Finding how far each prediction was from the result shows whether our predictions are getting better.

warmup.q: What do we call a guess with a reason, said before a test?
Is 'Which colour is the best?' a test question or an opinion?
warmup.a: An opinion. Each person's answer is true for them.

warmup.q: How did the pencil lift the bottle of rice?
warmup.a: The rice was packed tight, so it pressed on the pencil and friction held it.

warmup.q: Can you predict one coin toss for sure?
warmup.a: No. A coin lands by chance.

warmup.q: Who predicted that a comet would come back around 1758?
warmup.a: Edmond Halley. Nicole-Reine Lepaute helped work out the date more exactly.

warmup.q: Why do we say a prediction before the test, not after?
warmup.a: So the test can really show if we were right. After a test, anyone can say 'I knew it.'

science: Edmond Halley, A Synopsis of the Astronomy of Comets (1705): the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 were one comet, expected back around 1758.

Alexis Clairaut, with Jérôme Lalande and Nicole-Reine Lepaute, calculated the delay caused by Jupiter and Saturn (1757 to 1758) and predicted perihelion in mid-April 1759. Johann Georg Palitzsch saw the comet on 25 December 1758, and it passed closest to the Sun on 13 March 1759. Lalande credited Lepaute's part; Clairaut's published account did not name her.

Auguste Comte, Cours de philosophie positive (1835), on the chemical make-up of stars being unknowable; Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen, spectral analysis (1859 to 1860); Cecilia Payne, Stellar Atmospheres (1925).
Aryabhata, Aryabhatiya (499 CE), Gola section: eclipses explained by the Moon covering the Sun and by the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.
Karl Popper, Logik der Forschung (1934), on falsifiability.
Idli and dosa batter is leavened by lactic acid bacteria and yeasts, which make carbon dioxide; fermentation is much slower at fridge temperatures.
Granular friction: rice packed in a bottle can hold a pushed-in rod strongly enough to lift the bottle, because the packed grains press on the rod and on each other.

roots.context: We have sorted questions, made predictions and tested them with rice, coins and a die. Now we ask what the Rice Bottle Lift tells us about questions and answers.

deep_truth.truth: In the Rice Bottle Lift, you and your grown-up made different predictions. The bottle did the same thing in front of both of you. Anyone who repeats the test sees the same result. A question about which colour is best has no test, because each person's answer is true for them.
deep_truth.habit: We treat every question as the same kind: either you know the answer or you don't. But some questions are answered by a test that everyone sees the same way, and others by what each person likes or feels.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Rice Bottle Lift, two people made different predictions, and the bottle did the same thing in front of both of them. In the story Two Tumblers of Batter, Ila and Kiran mama both saw the same thing in the two tumblers. But 'idli or dosa?' had a different right answer for each person.

three.who_am_i: You are someone who can wonder, predict and test. Your likes, like your favourite colour, are part of you too.
three.what_is_life: Living beings get ready for what is coming. A young sunflower turns to face east during the night, ready for the morning sun.
three.what_is_this_world: The world answers our tests in the same way for everyone who tries. That is why people everywhere can share what they find.

roots.thread: In the Rice Bottle Lift, nobody's guess decided the answer. What decided it was how hard the rice grains pressed on the pencil. Everyone who watched saw the same result. Your liking for a colour is real too, but it is yours: another person can like a different colour.

teachings.teaching: A monk named Malunkyaputta asks the Buddha questions such as 'Is the world eternal?' The Buddha does not answer. He tells of a man hit by a poisoned arrow who refuses help until he knows who shot it. The man would die before the questions were answered. The Buddha says to work first on what can be worked on.
teachings.link: Some questions can be answered by a test today, and some cannot. Knowing which kind you have helps you choose what to do next.

teachings.teaching: Confucius tells his student: when you know a thing, say that you know it. When you do not know a thing, say that you do not know it. That is real knowing.
teachings.link: A prediction is said honestly before a test. When the test shows it was wrong, an honest person says so, and learns.

science.text: A test question is answered the same way for everyone who does the test carefully. That is why scientists in different countries can check each other's work.

Some questions, like what the stars are made of, looked untestable and were tested later. Others, like what the universe was like at its very start, may or may not ever be testable. Scientists argue about this.

other_view.view: Some philosophers say that even a test result is seen by each person in their own way, so no two people ever see exactly the same thing. Others answer that, even so, everyone who watched can agree that the bottle lifted.

practice.title: Predict your breath
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Before you breathe, predict: will this breath feel warm or cool on your top lip? Now breathe out through your nose and feel. Were you right? Now predict for a breath in: warm or cool? Breathe in slowly and feel what really happened. Do it three times.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Guess: will your breath feel warm or cool on your top lip? Breathe out and feel. Then guess again and breathe in.

how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years, people around the world saw comets as surprises. Many thought each comet came once and was a sign of bad times. In England, Edmond Halley studied old records. He saw that comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 had moved across the sky along almost the same path, about 76 years apart. In 1705 he wrote that they were one comet going round the Sun, and predicted it would come back around 1758. Halley died in 1742, before he could see if he was right. In France, Nicole-Reine Lepaute worked with Alexis Clairaut and Jérôme Lalande. For months they calculated how the pull of Jupiter and Saturn would slow the comet down. They predicted it would pass closest to the Sun in mid-April 1759. On Christmas night in 1758, a farmer in Germany named Johann Palitzsch spotted it. It passed closest to the Sun on 13 March 1759, about a month before the date they predicted. Clairaut later left Lepaute's name out of his book, but Lalande gave her the credit.
how_we_found_out.who: Edmond Halley, an English astronomer, and Nicole-Reine Lepaute, a French astronomer and calculator, with Alexis Clairaut and Jérôme Lalande
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Each comet comes once, passes by and never returns, often as a sign of bad times.
